Astro components are HTML-generating functions with a TypeScript frontmatter: props typed with interfaces, composition through slots, and a rendering model that disappears at runtime.

Chapter 1 called an `.astro` file an HTML-generating function, and that is true of components too — with one difference that changes everything about how you design them: after the build, the component *disappears*. There is no component tree in the browser, no reconciliation, no component state to manage. What remains is HTML. That single fact pushes Astro's component model toward a shape you may not have written before: components are closer to stamped-out parts in a factory than to objects in a running program. This chapter covers the three tools that model works with — typed props, slots, and the discipline of knowing which one a situation calls for. ## Components as HTML functions A component is a `.astro` file in `src/components` by convention, PascalCase by stronger convention, used as a tag: ```astro --- // src/components/Stat.astro interface Props { label: string; value: string; } const { label, value } = Astro.props; ---
{label}
{value}
``` Used on a page as ``, it produces one definition list row per instance and nothing else. There is no registration, no context, no import graph visible to the browser — `Stat` exists only during the build, produces one `
` per use, and evaporates. If you have written Rust, the feel is closer to a macro expanding than to an object being constructed. The upside of components that do not exist at runtime is freedom from a whole category of problems: no accidental state sharing between pages, no hydration bugs from duplicated trees, no render loops. The discipline it demands is the flip side: anything dynamic must either happen at build time, or be an island — Chapter 5's subject — or be a script, and the component API should make it obvious which of the three a caller is getting. ## Props with TypeScript Props are passed as attributes and read from `Astro.props`, and the type comes from an interface named `Props` that Astro understands by convention: ```astro --- // src/components/Alert.astro interface Props { severity: "info" | "warning" | "error"; message: string; dismissible?: boolean; } const { severity, message, dismissible = false } = Astro.props; ---

{message}

{dismissible && }
``` Three habits make props pleasant at any project size. Destructure immediately, giving required fields a type error when missing and optional fields a default, so callers only pass what they mean to. Use union types for closed sets — `"info" | "warning" | "error"` turns a typo into a build failure instead of a mystery class name. And keep `interface Props` as the single source of truth, because `astro check` (TypeScript over the whole project) validates every call site against it. A prop passed from a dynamic route's `props` object is checked the same way, which means the census in Chapter 2 and the component contract here join into one continuous type-checked pipeline from data to markup. ## Slots and composition Props are for data. Slots are for markup — and keeping the two apart is the component model's central design skill. A slot is a hole in the component; whatever the caller nests inside the tag lands there: ```astro --- // src/components/Card.astro interface Props { href: string; } const { href } = Astro.props; --- ``` The caller nests anything it likes inside the tag; the card's only job is the anchor and the hole: ```astro --- // used on a page import Card from "../components/Card.astro"; import Badge from "../components/Badge.astro"; ---

Servers, all the way down

Why we moved the render to the build machine.

 ``` The caller passed a heading, a paragraph, and another component — arbitrary markup, styled by the caller's own CSS, and the card never needed to know any of it. Try to imagine the prop version: a `title` string prop works, but the paragraph, the badge, the freedom to reorder? You would invent an escape hatch, then another. The escape hatch already exists, and it is the slot. If a component needs *content* rather than *configuration*, it is asking for a slot. ## Named and fallback slots Real components have more than one hole. `name="footer"` on the caller's markup fills a `` in the component; any slot with default content inside the tag keeps that content when the caller leaves it empty: ```astro --- // src/components/PostCard.astro interface Props { title: string; } const { title } = Astro.props; ---

{title}

Unpublished draft
``` ```astro --- import PostCard from "../components/PostCard.astro"; import AuthorChip from "../components/AuthorChip.astro"; ---

The default slot takes the body…

 ``` The fallback is not a prop default for strings — it is a whole chunk of markup, and it renders only when the caller provides nothing for that slot. This pairs naturally with layouts: a `DocsLayout` can define named slots for `header` and `sidebar` and a default slot for the page body, and every page using it opts into exactly the regions it has. Note the direction of knowledge flow: the component knows the *shape* of its regions, the caller knows the *content*, and neither knows more than it should. ## Passing markup, not just strings Here is the thing that isn't a thing: Astro has no mechanism for passing a rendered component or a template through a prop. Props are build-time values; markup is a slot. Coming from React, where `children` and render-props are the whole game, the temptation is to look for the equivalent — there isn't one, and the slot system is the equivalent, deliberately. ```astro --- // src/components/Callout.astro interface Props { kind?: "tip" | "warning"; } const { kind = "tip" } = Astro.props; ---
``` ```astro --- // src/pages/guide.astro — lists, code, other components: all fine in a slot import Callout from "../components/Callout.astro"; ---

Checklist for deleting a table:

  • Snapshot the volume
  • Announce in #deploys
 ``` There is one escape hatch worth knowing, if only to recognize it in the wild: inside a component, `Astro.slots.render("default")` returns the slot's content as an HTML string, which is how wrapper libraries forward content to scripts or transform it before emitting. Treat it as plumbing, not as a design pattern — the moment a component's prop list includes something like `bodyHtml`, you have reinvented the slot badly. The rule survives contact with real projects: **data crosses props; markup crosses slots**, and components that respect the boundary stay composable for years. ## Component APIs that age well The rendering model makes component design simpler than in SPA frameworks, because a component's entire behavior is visible in its own file. A few habits that hold up. Prefer slots over boolean props: `condensed` and `hideFooter` are each a future regret, while named slots let callers bring their own content and delete themselves when unused. Type everything, including the `Props` interface even when it has one field — the interface is the documentation that `astro check` enforces. Keep side effects at the edges: a component that fetches in its frontmatter is honest about being a build-time operation, but a component that fetches *and* formats *and* renders is three components wearing a trench coat, and its callers will re-render everything to change anything. ```astro --- // src/components/Quote.astro — small, typed, slotted: the whole API is visible interface Props { attribution?: string; } const { attribution } = Astro.props; --- ``` That component is a good endpoint: one optional prop, one slot, no state to guess at. When a component grows past roughly a screen, split it by region — the slot boundaries you already have are natural seam lines. And when a component genuinely needs interactivity, do not grow logic into it; make it the static shell around an island, which keeps the zero-JS default intact and keeps this chapter's model clean. Islands have rules of their own, and they are next. ## Key takeaways - Astro components are HTML-generating functions that exist only at build time, so their design space is build-time composition, not runtime state. - Declare `interface Props`, destructure `Astro.props` with defaults, and use union types so every call site is checked against the contract at build. - Slots are for markup and props are for data — if a caller is passing content, it wants a slot, and there is deliberately no way to pass rendered markup as a prop. - Named slots with fallback content give components multiple optional regions, which is how layouts offer headers, sidebars, and bodies without boolean flags. - Small, typed, slotted components with visible APIs age well; grow interactivity by wrapping islands, never by accumulating flags and lifecycle logic. One special kind of content deserves its own machinery, though — the markdown and MDX that make up blogs and docs. Next chapter: content collections, the feature the rest of this book leans on.
content-first sites, islands, and zero JS by default

Astro starts as pure HTML and adds JavaScript only where you ask for it. This chapter builds the mental model — islands, zero-JS-by-default, and why content-first sites get faster when the framework does less.

For twenty years the frontend has swung on a pendulum. One end is the multi-page site: every click a full page load, every page HTML served straight from a server, the browser doing what browsers were built to do. The other end is the single-page app: one download, one runtime, navigation rendered in JavaScript. Through the 2010s the pendulum swung hard toward SPAs, and a generation of tooling quietly assumed every site wants to be one. Then something awkward became impossible to ignore: most of what we build is not an app. It is a landing page, a changelog, a blog, a set of docs — and shipping a JavaScript runtime to a visitor's phone so it can render eight hundred words of pricing copy is an expensive way to show text. You already ship software — React at work, Svelte when you get to choose, Rust and Tauri when the job wants a real binary — so you know what a framework costs and when it pays for itself. Astro is built around a different default: **a page is HTML, generated at build time, delivered with zero JavaScript unless one specific component asks for it.** Everything in this book — routing, content collections, islands, actions — is machinery attached to that default, so this chapter builds the mental model carefully. ## Why Astro exists Every framework answers one question first: where and when does your page get rendered? React answers "in the browser, after the runtime loads." Next.js and SvelteKit soften that with server rendering, but the page still needs the runtime to hydrate before it is fully alive. Astro answers differently: *at build time, to finished HTML, by default*. The work happens once, on the build machine, and visitors get the answer already baked in. ```astro --- // src/pages/changelog.astro — this frontmatter runs at build time const res = await fetch("https://api.example.com/v2/releases"); const releases = await res.json(); ---

Changelog

    {releases.slice(0, 5).map((release) => (
  • {release.tag_name} — {release.name}
    • ))}
``` ```html

Changelog

  • v2.4.0 — server islands land
  • v2.3.1 — fix: sticky header overlap
  • v2.3.0 — new import pipeline
``` The API call ran once, during the build, on a machine you control. The visitor's browser never hears about it: no skeleton, no spinner, no client-side fetch. This is the whole thesis in one move — **every unit of work you shift from runtime to build time is a unit the visitor's device doesn't spend.** A framework that does less isn't a lesser framework; for content-first sites it is simply the right one. ## Zero JavaScript by default Take the default seriously, because most frameworks don't have one. When Astro builds the page above, the output is HTML and CSS and nothing else. No runtime is downloaded. No hydration pass re-executes your components in the browser. The frontmatter ran on the build machine, the template was consumed into markup, and the `.astro` file itself never leaves your repository. The consequences compound. Content renders the moment HTML arrives, because there is no render-blocking bundle ahead of it in the queue. The page works with JavaScript disabled, throttled, or broken by an aggressive privacy extension. Hosting is trivial — the output is files, which any CDN serves at the edge. And on a three-year-old Android phone over hotel Wi-Fi, your site is just as fast as it is on your laptop, because the device does almost no work. ```text GET / index.html 14 kB GET /_astro/home.css stylesheet 9 kB GET /fonts/body.woff2 font 34 kB GET /_astro/hero.avif image 88 kB JavaScript — 0 kB ``` That last line is the feature. It is also the budget: the moment you add JavaScript, you are choosing to add it, component by component, rather than accepting it as the cost of admission. The next chapter's file-based router and most of this book's features run entirely inside that zero-JS envelope. ## Islands architecture Zero JS by default raises the obvious objection: real pages have parts that need JavaScript — a search box, a cart widget, a chart. Astro's answer is *islands architecture*, and it is the load-bearing metaphor for the whole book. A page is a sea of static HTML; the few components that genuinely need script ship their own JavaScript and become interactive on their own schedule. The sea around them stays free. ```astro --- // src/pages/products/[id].astro import ProductGallery from "../../components/ProductGallery.svelte"; import AddToCart from "../../components/AddToCart.svelte"; import { getProduct } from "../../lib/catalog"; const product = await getProduct(Astro.params.id); ---

{product.name}

{product.description}

``` That `client:visible` attribute is a *hydration directive*: it tells Astro to ship this component's JavaScript and wake it up when it scrolls into view, and to leave everything else alone. The gallery hydrates itself; the description, the reviews, and the footer never pay a byte for it. You will meet the full set of directives and their trade-offs in Chapter 5. For now, hold the shape: interactivity is opt-in, local, and each island pays only its own cost. ## The MPA renaissance The old objection to multi-page sites was that full page loads feel slow — and in 2015, they did. Three things have changed since. Browsers got smarter: modern engines speculatively prefetch links in the viewport, so by the time you click, the next page is often already in cache. Hosting got fast: HTML on a CDN edge is frequently delivered before a SPA's data fetch would have resolved. And the View Transitions API now lets the browser animate the swap between two full documents, erasing the white flash that made MPAs feel cheap. Astro leans into the browser instead of replacing it. Its client router — opt-in, a few kilobytes, covered in Chapter 8 — intercepts navigations, fetches the next page's HTML, and swaps it in with persisted state and animated transitions. It is not a JavaScript runtime; it is a thin broker between the pages you already have. SPAs won partly because MPAs felt janky, and the platform has spent a decade fixing the jank. When the documents themselves are cheap, the browser's native machinery is hard to beat. ## Anatomy of an .astro file Every `.astro` file has two halves, separated by a code fence. The top — the *frontmatter* — is TypeScript that runs at build time or on the server, never in the browser: imports, data fetching, computation. Below the fence is the template: HTML with `{expression}` placeholders. The expressions are template syntax, not a virtual DOM. There is no diffing and no re-render, because the file describes exactly one rendering of one page. ```astro --- // src/pages/team.astro import TeamMember from "../components/TeamMember.astro"; const res = await fetch("https://api.example.com/v2/team"); const team = await res.json(); const current = team.filter((member) => !member.alumni); --- The team {current.length === 0 &&

Nobody here yet.

} {current.map((member) => ( ))} ``` Components are imported in the frontmatter and used as tags in the template — and the whole file is an HTML-generating function that disappears after the build. View source on the deployed page and you see the result, not the framework: no runtime namespace, no hydration annotations, no component tree serialized into the wire. Coming from React or Svelte, the discipline is that the frontmatter has no lifecycle and no state; if a value can be computed at build, this is the place it gets computed. ## When Astro fits (and when it doesn't) Astro's home turf is anything whose unit of delivery is a *page*: marketing sites, blogs, documentation, changelogs, portfolios, catalogs, help centers. It is equally strong at the common hybrid — a content site with a few app-like corners. That is exactly what islands are for, and a page with 95 percent static content plus one search island is the framework operating at design capacity: ```astro --- import SearchDialog from "../components/SearchDialog.svelte"; import { getCollection } from "astro:content"; const docs = await getCollection("docs"); ---
d.data)} />
``` Now the honest part: some sites are not pages. An auth-gated dashboard where every screen is a live, stateful view — optimistic updates, websockets, deeply shared client state — will not benefit, because every route is an island and you have rebuilt an SPA with extra ceremony. Reach for Next.js or SvelteKit there, or Tauri when the app wants to be a desktop app. The fit test is a ratio: count the routes that are *documents* and the routes that are *app views*. If documents win, Astro wins. If they don't, no amount of zero-JS default will save you from the framework you actually need. ## Key takeaways - Astro renders pages to finished HTML at build time, so visitors receive documents rather than a runtime plus instructions for assembling one. - Zero JavaScript by default is a budget, not a limitation: interactivity is added per component and each addition pays its own cost. - Islands are the core mental model — static HTML everywhere, with script-carrying components waking up on their own schedule via hydration directives. - The MPA is competitive again because browsers prefetch, CDNs serve HTML from the edge, and view transitions smooth the swaps; Chapter 8 covers Astro's client router. - An `.astro` file is an HTML-generating function: TypeScript frontmatter computes, the template renders, and neither ships to the browser. - Fit is a ratio of documents to app views: content-first sites are Astro's strength, while state-heavy, auth-gated dashboards belong to SPA frameworks. Next: the router. In Astro it is your file tree, and the structure you choose in the first hour is the one you live with in production.

Content collections give every markdown and MDX file a schema, a type, and a query API — the load-bearing feature behind blogs, docs, and changelogs. This is the chapter the rest of the book leans on.
Astro's router is your file tree. Pages, layouts, dynamic routes with getStaticPaths, redirects, and 404s — the structural skeleton every Astro project hangs on.

Astro's router is your file tree: a file in `src/pages` becomes a URL, a directory becomes a path segment, and square brackets become dynamic parameters. If you have used file-based routing in Next.js or SvelteKit, this is home turf — but Astro's version has fewer knobs, and the knobs it has are the ones that age well. That matters more than it sounds, because routing is the skeleton of a project: decisions made in the first hour outlive the component library, the styling approach, and usually the developer who made them. This chapter builds that skeleton — pages, layouts, dynamic routes — and then works the edges where mistakes get expensive: catch-alls, 404s, and redirects. ## The project skeleton `npm create astro@latest` gives you a tree with strong opinions baked in, and it is worth internalizing what each directory is *for* before you fight it: ```text my-site/ ├── astro.config.mjs → integrations, adapters, build options ├── public/ → copied verbatim: favicon, robots.txt, static fonts ├── src/ │ ├── assets/ → images processed by astro:assets (Chapter 7) │ ├── components/ → .astro components and framework islands │ ├── content/ → content collections: markdown and MDX (Chapter 4) │ ├── layouts/ → page shells: BaseLayout, PostLayout, DocsLayout │ ├── pages/ → the router lives here │ └── styles/ → global CSS └── package.json ``` The load-bearing distinction is `src` versus `public`. Everything in `src` is processed by Vite: imported, transformed, hashed, bundled. Everything in `public` is copied to the output byte-for-byte, no questions asked. The practical rule: if a file needs a build step or a stable hashed URL — fonts you will preload, images that get optimized — it belongs in `src`. If it must be reachable under exactly the name you gave it, like `public/favicon.svg`, it belongs in `public`. Almost every early confusion about "where does this file go" dissolves once you ask which of those two jobs it has. ## Pages become routes Every file in `src/pages` maps to a URL by path, with the extension stripped and one special case: `index` means "the root of this directory." ```text src/pages/index.astro → / src/pages/about.astro → /about src/pages/blog/index.astro → /blog src/pages/blog/first-post.md → /blog/first-post src/pages/docs/setup.mdx → /docs/setup ``` Markdown and MDX files are routes too, which is worth pausing on: a blog can literally be a folder of `.md` files with no dynamic route at all. A markdown page receives its own frontmatter as props and renders through a layout it names in that frontmatter — so for a handful of flat documents, the file *is* the site. The moment you want listing pages, sorting, or shared metadata rules, you graduate to content collections and a dynamic route, which is the Chapter 4 pattern we will use for the rest of the book. Keep pages themselves thin either way: a page's job is to say which layout renders here and where its content comes from, nothing more. ## Layouts as the outer shell A layout is not a framework feature — it is a plain Astro component that wraps a `` and lives in `src/layouts` by convention. That convention is worth keeping, because it gives you a greppable answer to "where does the `` tag live": ```astro --- // src/layouts/BaseLayout.astro interface Props { title: string; description?: string; } const { title, description = "A site built with Astro" } = Astro.props; --- {title}
``` ```astro --- // src/pages/about.astro import BaseLayout from "../layouts/BaseLayout.astro"; ---

About

The page content lands in the slot.

 ``` Everything global belongs here: the favicon, fonts, analytics, the client router when you adopt it in Chapter 8. The `Props` interface is doing real work — every page that forgets a required title fails the type check at build time, not as a missing tag in production. Slots, named slots, and the full composition model get their own chapter next; for now, notice only that the layout is just a component whose one special ability is having a hole in the middle. ## Dynamic routes and getStaticPaths Most interesting routes are not one file per page; they are one file per *kind* of page. Square brackets make a route dynamic: `src/pages/blog/[slug].astro` matches `/blog/whatever`, and the file decides which slugs actually exist. ```astro --- // src/pages/blog/[slug].astro import { getCollection, render } from "astro:content"; import BaseLayout from "../../layouts/BaseLayout.astro"; export async function getStaticPaths() { const posts = await getCollection("blog"); return posts.map((post) => ({ params: { slug: post.id }, props: { post }, })); } const { post } = Astro.props; const { Content } = await render(post); ---
``` `getStaticPaths` is the census. In static output every URL must exist at build time, so this function runs once per build and returns one route per object it produces: `params` fills in the bracket, `props` hands data to the page without a second query. If a blog post's frontmatter is broken or a fetch fails, the build fails — loudly, with the offending entry named. That is static generation's price and its gift: errors happen on your machine, before anything is deployed, instead of as a 500 on someone's phone. When a route truly cannot be known at build time, Chapter 6 shows the per-page escape hatch. ## Rest params, 404s, and redirects Three edges round out the system. A *rest parameter* — `[...slug]` with three dots — matches any depth, which is how you build a catch-all for nested docs or a legacy URL sweeper: ```astro --- // src/pages/docs/[...path].astro export async function getStaticPaths() { return [ { params: { path: "guides/install" } }, { params: { path: "guides/install/advanced" } }, ]; } --- ``` The 404 is not special either: a page named `404.astro` in `src/pages` is served by every major host whenever nothing else matches. Treat it as a real page, because lost visitors are real users: ```astro --- // src/pages/404.astro import BaseLayout from "../layouts/BaseLayout.astro"; ---

404

That page moved or never existed. The home page is a good start.

 ``` Rest params are greedy and match anything, so put them last in their directory and let `getStaticPaths` decide what they actually resolve to; the built 404 is your safety net for everything the census did not name. ## Routing decisions that age well Routing choices are cheap to make and expensive to reverse, because every decision leaks into URLs that other people have bookmarked. A few opinions from production. Keep one dynamic route per content type, and name params after what they carry — `[slug]` for a human-readable post, `[id]` only when the id genuinely is the identifier — because the bracket shows up in the URL forever. Prefer real redirects over JavaScript redirects: the config below issues actual HTTP redirects at the host level, which is the cheapest possible respect for inbound links and lets you reorganize content without breaking anyone. ```js // astro.config.mjs import { defineConfig } from "astro/config"; export default defineConfig({ trailingSlash: "never", build: { format: "directory" }, redirects: { "/twitter": "https://example.com/@yourhandle", "/old-post": "/blog/renamed-post", }, }); ``` Pick a trailing-slash setting and never think about it again — the default of `"ignore"` works, but an explicit choice prevents a future of duplicate-content debates. `build.format: "directory"` gives every page its own directory with an `index.html`, which hosts and CDNs handle most gracefully. And pass entry objects through `props` rather than re-fetching inside the page: the census already did the work once, and a route that quietly queries the world again for each page is where builds start to hurt. Chapter 4 builds on exactly this shape, with collections feeding `getStaticPaths` instead of ad-hoc file reads. ## Key takeaways - The router is `src/pages`: files become URLs by path, `index` files become directory roots, and the `src` versus `public` split decides what gets processed versus copied. - Layouts are ordinary components with a `` in the middle, stored in `src/layouts` by convention, and they are the right home for every global concern. - `getStaticPaths` is a build-time census: `params` shape the URL, `props` carry the data, and a broken entry fails the build instead of production. - Rest params like `[...path]` match any depth for catch-alls, `404.astro` handles misses, and config-level redirects keep old URLs alive without JavaScript. - Routing decisions leak into permanent URLs, so name params honestly, fix trailing slashes once, and never make the page re-query what the census already fetched. The skeleton is in place, but routes are only half the story — the components that fill them have their own rules, and slots are the mechanism that makes them compose. That is next.
adding JavaScript exactly where it pays

client:visible, client:idle, client:load — hydration directives let Svelte, React, or Vue components ship as isolated islands in a sea of static HTML. Islands are Astro's core trade: interactivity on demand, nothing else.

Chapter 1 promised that interactivity is opt-in and pays its own way. This chapter is where you learn the exchange rate. Islands are Astro's core trade: a component ships its framework and hydrates in the browser, everything around it ships nothing, and you decide component by component which is which. Since you already write Svelte and React, the components themselves will be familiar ground — the new material is the *boundary*: what crosses it, when the island wakes up, and when a plain script is the better tool for the job. ## The cost of hydration Hydration is the price SPA frameworks pay for server rendering: the HTML arrives, and then the framework downloads, boots, re-runs your components, and re-attaches event listeners so the page becomes interactive. The output HTML was free; making it *alive* is not. A modest React page ships the framework itself before any of your code, and the whole bundle executes on the visitor's device regardless of how little of the page actually responds to input. ```text What a typical hydrated page ships before it is interactive: react + react-dom ~45 kB gzip your component tree 30-120 kB gzip state + data layer 10-40 kB gzip ``` The waste is structural, not a sign of doing it wrong: in a hydrated app, *every* component pays the framework cost whether it is interactive or not. Islands invert the accounting. The static 95 percent of the page is HTML with no framework attached, and the framework cost is charged only to the components that genuinely need it — and only at the moment they need it. ## Your first island An island is any framework component rendered inside an `.astro` file with a hydration directive. Here is an upvote button in Svelte 5 — unremarkable by your standards, which is the point: ```svelte ``` Using it is two lines: an import in the frontmatter, a directive on the tag. ```astro --- // src/pages/blog/[slug].astro import Upvote from "../../components/Upvote.svelte"; ---

A completely static article

Every byte of this prose ships as plain HTML…

``` The directive is doing all the work. `client:visible` tells Astro to render the button's initial HTML at build time like everything else, ship the Svelte runtime and this component only if the button is on screen, and hydrate it when it scrolls into view. The article around it — however long — pays nothing. You can render the same component ten times on a page and the runtime ships once; the islands share the framework, not the work. ## The client directives There are five directives, and each answers one question: *when does this island's JavaScript download and execute?* ```astro ``` `client:load` hydrates as soon as the page loads — for controls the user will reach for immediately. `client:idle` waits for the browser to be idle via `requestIdleCallback` — good for things wanted soon but not first, like a theme toggle. `client:visible` waits for the island to enter the viewport — the workhorse for pages where content scrolls and the interactive part is below the fold. `client:media` hydrates only when a media query matches — a mobile-only menu never touches a desktop visitor's network. `client:only` skips server-side rendering entirely: the island renders only in the browser, useful when a component depends on `window` or draws differently every time, at the cost of an empty placeholder until it loads. Every directive except `client:only` still server-renders the initial HTML, so the page never flashes empty where content could have been. The choice is a small scheduling decision, and it is worth making deliberately because the default temptation — `client:load` on everything — quietly reintroduces the waterfall islands were invented to avoid. The decision tree in practice: does the user need it on first paint, like a nav search? Then `client:load`. Is it needed soon but not first? `client:idle`. Is it below the fold or off in a tab? `client:visible`, and most islands in content-heavy sites are this one. Does it only exist on one breakpoint? `client:media`. Does it render nothing useful on the server? `client:only`, and pay for it knowingly. ```astro --- import MobileNav from "../components/MobileNav.svelte"; import NewsletterForm from "../components/NewsletterForm.svelte"; ---
``` The habit that keeps pages fast: pick the *latest* moment the island can wake up without the user noticing. A newsletter form in the footer hydrated on idle is indistinguishable from one hydrated on load — except on a slow phone, where it isn't. ## Frameworks inside Astro Islands are framework-agnostic, and mixing frameworks on one page is a supported configuration, not a hack. Install the integration once — `npx astro add react`, `npx astro add vue` — and the directives work identically on any framework's components: ```astro --- import LikeButton from "../components/LikeButton"; import Upvote from "../components/Upvote.svelte"; --- ``` The React component needs no changes to become an island — same props, same hooks, same testing story you already have. Each island carries only its own framework's runtime, so a Svelte island costs a couple of kilobytes while a React island costs the React baseline; that difference is a legitimate factor when choosing what to write new islands in. What you should avoid is frameworks *hydrating each other's territory* — an island is self-contained by design, and passing state between islands is your signal to reconsider the boundary rather than build a bridge. ## Passing props to islands Props cross the island boundary by being serialized into the HTML that ships, then revived in the browser. That constrains the shape: JSON-shaped values — strings, numbers, booleans, plain objects and arrays — plus a few structured types Astro knows how to serialize, like `Date`, `Map`, and `Set`. Functions and class instances do not cross: ```astro --- import AddToCart from "../components/AddToCart.svelte"; const product = { sku: "nb-2025", name: "Field Notebook", price: 14, tags: ["paper", "grid"], }; --- ``` The type checker still validates the props against `AddToCart`'s declared types — but the runtime constraint is serialization, not TypeScript. In practice two patterns cover the gaps. Big data: don't pass it; pass an id and let the island fetch what it needs when it wakes up. Behavior: don't pass callbacks; pass configuration. An island that receives `onSave` as a prop is a component that has outgrown the boundary — restructure it so the island owns its behavior and the static page owns its placement. ## Scripts without islands Before reaching for an island, ask whether the behavior needs a framework at all. A ` ``` That is a genuinely interactive component — state changes, event listeners, feedback to the user — with no framework and no hydration. The rule of thumb: if the behavior is a few lines of DOM work with no meaningful state, a script is lighter than an island in bytes, complexity, and honesty. If there is real state, re-rendering, or framework components inside, use an island. Use `is:inline` to opt out of processing when you need a raw, un-bundled script exactly where you wrote it — third-party embeds are the usual reason. ## Third-party scripts with partytown The heaviest scripts on many sites are ones you didn't write: analytics, tag managers, A/B testing. They land on the main thread and contend with everything you shipped, which is a bitter trade for code that exists to measure your site. *Partytown* relocates third-party scripts into a web worker, off the main thread entirely, with DOM access proxied behind the scenes: ```astro --- // src/layouts/BaseLayout.astro import { Partytown } from "@qwik.dev/partytown/react"; --- ``` The `type="text/partytown"` attribute is the whole trick: the browser ignores the script as JavaScript, and the worker executes it. Calls your page makes into the analytics API — the `forward` list — are shuttled to the worker so the integration behaves normally. Cost is one component and a few kilobytes; benefit is a main thread that belongs to your users. It composes cleanly with everything in this chapter: islands for the interactivity you chose, partytown for the scripts you didn't. ## Key takeaways - Hydration charges the whole page for the framework; islands charge only the components that are interactive, and only when they wake up. - The five directives are a scheduling menu — `load`, `idle`, `visible`, `media`, `only` — and the right choice is the latest wake-up the user won't notice. - Svelte, React, and Vue components become islands without modification; each ships only its own runtime, and mixing frameworks on a page is supported. - Props must be serializable: pass data and configuration across the boundary, fetch big data inside the island, and never pass functions. - A processed, deduplicated `

Svelte is a compiler that writes your event listeners, DOM updates, and reactive plumbing at build time — then disappears. This chapter builds the mental model for Svelte 5, where reactivity is language, not library.

Every frontend framework answers the same question: when your data changes, how does the view find out? React's answer is a runtime — render the tree into a virtual DOM, diff it against the previous render, patch the differences. Vue's answer is proxies that intercept every read and write; Angular's is a scheduler walking a dependency graph of its own. Each of these answers ships machinery to the browser, and the browser loads it, parses it, and runs it on every interaction for the life of the app. Svelte's answer is different: **the framework is a compiler.** You write components, a build step turns them into small, direct JavaScript that updates the DOM exactly where needed, and at runtime there is almost nothing left to load. That one design decision explains most of what follows in this book: why components are files, why reactivity looks like language rather than library calls, why bundles stay small, and where the tradeoffs land. This chapter builds that mental model before we go deep on any syntax. ## The framework paradox A framework earns its place by solving real problems. It gives you components to compose, a declarative mapping from state to UI, and a disciplined path from event to update. Writing those by hand means `addEventListener` bookkeeping, string templating, and update code that drifts out of sync with the markup it serves — problems nobody should solve fresh in every project. But there is a paradox hiding in the usual implementations. Nearly everything a framework does at runtime is *determinable at build time*. Which element listens to which event, which text nodes depend on which values, which parts of the tree change together — the compiler can see all of it in your source. A runtime framework re-derives those facts on every render, on every user's machine, forever. That is the paradox: we ship a general-purpose interpreter to the browser when a specific-purpose program could be generated ahead of time. Svelte takes the second path — do the general work once, during the build, and ship only the result. ## A compiler that writes your boilerplate The quickest way to feel the difference is the smallest interesting component: a counter. First, the React you already know: ```jsx // React: describe the tree; the runtime reconciles it import { useState } from 'react'; export default function Counter() { const [count, setCount] = useState(0); return ( ); } ``` Nothing is wrong with this code, and that is the point — it is perfectly ordinary. Now the same component in Svelte: ```svelte ``` Same shape, same behavior — and no reconciliation. When you build this file, the compiler generates an event listener wired to exactly one button and an update that rewrites exactly one text node. It wrote the boilerplate you would have written by hand in vanilla JavaScript, then removed itself from the bundle. That is the honest version of the phrase you may have heard: *Svelte is a compiler that disappears.* ## Reactivity as language: runes The counter's `let count = $state(0)` is the whole philosophy in one line. `$state` is not a function you import; it is a compiler keyword. The `$` prefix marks it as something the compiler rewrites, and the rewrite attaches reactivity to the variable itself — when `count` changes, every part of the UI that reads it updates, with no subscriber lists for you to maintain. Svelte 5 has a handful of these keywords, called *runes*: `$state` declares mutable state, `$derived` declares values computed from it, `$effect` runs side effects after the DOM updates, `$props` receives what a parent passed in, and snippets make markup composable. Chapters 2 through 5 cover them properly; Chapter 1 only needs you to recognize the shape. One orienting note if you met Svelte before version 5: the old model made reactivity *implicit* — a plain top-level `let` was silently reactive, and a `$:` label computed values from it. Runes make the same machinery explicit and portable. Reactivity is now something you declare, in components and outside them, rather than something the compiler infers from where a variable sits. Everything in this book uses the runes syntax; the old forms are worth recognizing only so you can migrate away from them. At a glance, the whole vocabulary you will spend four chapters on: ```svelte ``` ## Anatomy of a .svelte file A component is a single file with up to three sections: ```svelte

hello {name}

``` Three things deserve notice. The markup is genuinely HTML — there is no JSX dialect to learn, and event attributes like `onclick` carry the DOM's own names. The braces in `{name}` are the only syntax you need to embed a value, and they are compiled away, not evaluated at runtime by an interpreter. And the styles are *scoped*: the compiler rewrites each selector so it can only match this component's elements, so one file's CSS cannot leak into another's. The sections use the language of their domain — JavaScript in the script, CSS in the style block — and everything between them stays honest HTML. ## What the compiler emits Svelte's output is worth a look, because knowing what ships changes how you think about cost. A simplified sketch of what the counter compiles to: ```js // greatly simplified: the shape of compiled Svelte import { template, open, text, set_text } from 'svelte/internal/client'; export default function Counter(anchor) { // count becomes a signal: a value plus a list of dependents let count = $.signal(0); const button = open(template(``), anchor); const label = text(button); set_text(label, () => `clicked ${count.value} times`); button.addEventListener('click', () => (count.value += 1)); } ``` The real output is denser and handles edge cases this sketch hides, but the shape is true to life. There is no virtual DOM and no diffing: the compiler already knows which text node depends on `count`, so the update touches exactly that node. This is why Svelte apps stay small — you pay for the features you use, once, in generated code, instead of carrying a runtime's entire surface area in the hope you might need it. ## Where Svelte fits in your stack An honest word on tradeoffs: Svelte's ecosystem is smaller than React's. Fewer turnkey component libraries, fewer prebuilt integrations, fewer answers on the second page of search results. The core — state, transitions, SvelteKit — is polished and stable, but if your project leans on a niche React-only library, that dependency effectively chooses your framework. Svelte is the right default when you value small bundles, readable components, and a compiler that catches mistakes at build time; it is the wrong default when your team lives inside React-specific tooling. It also composes well with what you already run. SvelteKit, the app framework, is Chapter 8's subject and the standard way to build anything with routing or a server. But Svelte is not only SvelteKit: it drops into plain Vite for embeds and widgets, renders as islands inside Astro, and is a first-class UI layer for Tauri — so a Rust core can ship behind a Svelte front end in the same shell you already build with Cargo. Starting a project is one command either way: ```bash npx sv create my-app # SvelteKit: routing, server, adapters included npm create vite@latest -- --template svelte # or: bare Svelte for embeds cd my-app && npm run dev ``` The compiler mental model travels; the rest of this book assumes it. ## Key takeaways - Svelte moves framework work from runtime to build time: the compiler generates your DOM updates and event wiring, so the browser loads results rather than machinery. - A `.svelte` file has three sections — script, markup, style — and the compiler scopes the styles to the component automatically. - Runes such as `$state` and `$derived` are compiler keywords, not imports; they make reactivity explicit and replace the older implicit model wholesale. - There is no virtual DOM: compiled components update exactly the nodes that depend on changed values, which is where the size and speed wins come from. - The tradeoff is ecosystem breadth; the compensation is that Svelte slots into SvelteKit, Astro islands, Vite embeds, and Tauri shells without ceremony. Next up: the runes themselves, starting with the one every component begins with — `$state`.
Template blocks that compile to tight imperative code — conditionals, keyed lists, and await — plus bind: for two-way binding on inputs, components, and media elements.

You have components, state, and props. What remains before you can build interfaces is template syntax: how a view decides what to show, how it renders collections, and how it keeps inputs and state in sync. Svelte's answer is a small set of *blocks* — `{#if}`, `{#each}`, `{#await}`, `{#key}` — and the `bind:` directive. Like everything else in this book, none of it survives to the browser as an interpreter: blocks compile down to plain conditionals and loops operating on the DOM. ## Templates that compile Svelte's template syntax is worth approaching the way Chapter 1 approached the compiler: as instructions to a code generator, not API calls. When you write an `{#if}` block, the compiler emits an actual `if` statement; when you write `{#each}`, it emits a loop that creates, moves, and removes the nodes each item owns. There is no virtual DOM diffing these decisions after the fact, which is why Svelte templates stay fast without memoization rituals. The blocks also keep templates honest about structure. Every block opens with `#`, continues with `:`, and closes with `/` — `{#if}`, `{:else}`, `{/if}` — so the shape of the control flow is visible at a glance in the markup, the same way Rust's `match` arms make branching impossible to misread. We will cover conditionals, lists, and await here, and leave transitions — motion attached to these same blocks — for Chapter 7. ## Conditionals with if and else The `{#if}` block renders its contents only while a condition holds, with optional `{:else if}` chains and a final `{:else}`: ```svelte {#if count === 0}

go on, click it

{:else if count > 10}

that is a lot of clicks

{:else}

clicked {count} times

{/if} ``` The important semantic: an `{#if}` block *creates and destroys* its contents — it does not toggle a `display: none`. When the condition flips, the old branch's elements are removed from the DOM and the new branch's are built, running any cleanups and transitions on the way. That is usually what you want, because state that only matters in one branch is not kept alive behind the scenes. When you do want elements to stay mounted but hidden, that is a CSS decision, and an explicit one: put the class on the element yourself. ## Lists, keys, and each The `{#each}` block renders a collection, and the *key* in parentheses tells the compiler how to tell items apart: ```svelte
    {#each todos as todo, index (todo.id)}
  • {index + 1}. {todo.title}
    • {:else}
  • nothing to do
    • {/each}
``` The key `(todo.id)` is an identity claim: when the array reorders or an item is removed in the middle, the compiler moves and patches the existing DOM nodes instead of rebuilding from indexes. Without a key, `{#each}` falls back to index-based matching, which silently scrambles per-item state — input values, transitions, local component state — whenever the array shifts. Key by a stable id, never by index, the same rule as every other framework's list rendering. The `{:else}` branch renders when the list is empty, `index` is optional, and you can destructure inline: `{#each todos as { title, done } (title)}`. ## Await and key blocks The `{#await}` block renders the three states of a promise as first-class template syntax: ```svelte {#await reportPromise}

loading report…

{:then report} {:catch error}

{error.message}

{/await} ``` Each state gets its own markup, the latest promise wins if the value changes mid-flight, and there is no loading flag to forget. It pairs naturally with SvelteKit's `load` functions in Chapter 8, where data usually arrives before the component renders — but for client-side fetches triggered by user action, `{#await}` keeps the states honest. Its sibling `{#key expression}` destroys and recreates its contents whenever the expression changes — useful to reset a component's internal state, restart a transition, or re-run an entrance animation when an id changes: ```svelte {#key userId} {/key} ``` ## bind:value and friends Forms are where one-way data flow turns into ceremony, so Svelte makes two-way wiring a directive: `bind:value` keeps an input and a `$state` variable in sync, in both directions, without you writing the update handler. ```svelte {#each ['sprinkles', 'fudge'] as extra} {/each} ``` The directive is type-aware: inputs of type `number` and `range` coerce to real numbers, checkboxes pair with `bind:checked`, and `bind:group` collects the checked values of a radio or checkbox set into one array. Underneath, the compiler writes exactly the `input` and `change` listeners you would have written — which is to say, `bind:` is not magic, it is generated plumbing, and it composes with the reactivity from Chapter 2: assigning to the bound variable updates the input, and typing updates the variable. ## Binding components with $bindable Props flow down by default, and Chapter 3 argued that is a virtue. Sometimes, though, a component wants to offer the same two-way ergonomics as an input. The `$bindable` rune opts a prop in: ```svelte ``` ```svelte

{volume}%

``` Inside `Volume`, `value` is an ordinary mutable prop — assigning it notifies whoever bound to it. The `$bindable(50)` default applies when the parent passes nothing and does not bind. The discipline worth keeping: reach for `bind:` on components for form-like state where the two-way reading is the truth, and prefer callback props from Chapter 3 for events that *mean* something — submitting, confirming, deleting. Bindings say "this is shared state"; callbacks say "this happened." ## Media and element bindings The `bind:` family extends past forms to elements themselves. Media elements expose playback state, and elements expose geometry: ```svelte

{time.toFixed(1)}s of {duration.toFixed(1)}s

``` `bind:this` captures the element itself into a variable — the escape hatch for calling DOM APIs directly, which we will use in Chapter 5 for canvas and focus management. `bind:currentTime`, `bind:paused`, and friends are live, writable views of the element's state, so setting `paused` really plays or pauses the video. Read-only bindings like `bind:clientWidth` and `bind:offsetHeight` publish an element's measured geometry as reactive values, which replaces a whole category of resize-observer boilerplate. As always, the compiler wrote the listeners; you wrote the intent. ## Key takeaways - Template blocks compile to real conditionals and loops — there is no runtime interpretation of `{#if}` or `{#each}`. - `{#if}` creates and destroys DOM rather than hiding it; keep that in mind when state should or should not survive a branch flip. - Key your `{#each}` blocks by stable id, or per-item state scrambles when the array reorders; `{:else}` handles the empty case. - `bind:value`, `bind:group`, and `bind:checked` are two-way wiring for forms; `$bindable` opts a component prop into the same ergonomics. - `bind:this` captures elements for direct DOM access, media bindings publish playback state, and geometry bindings replace resize-observer boilerplate. One warning stays from this chapter: state you can write from two directions needs discipline about *when* work happens in response. That is effects — the next chapter.

the stack, the heap, and who cleans up
Every value in Rust has exactly one owner, and when the owner goes, the value goes with it. This single rule replaces garbage collection and manual free — and it changes how you design everything.

Every language has to answer the same question: when a value is created on the heap, who is responsible for releasing it? C answers "you, the programmer" — which is fast, and which has produced four decades of use-after-free bugs. Java and Go answer "the runtime" — which is safe, and which costs you a garbage collector, its pauses, and its memory overhead. Rust gives a third answer: **the compiler proves, at compile time, that every value has exactly one owner, and inserts the cleanup code for you.**

That answer is called *ownership*, and it is not one feature among many. It is the load-bearing wall of the entire language. Memory safety, the borrow checker, fearless concurrency, even why `String` behaves differently from `&str` — all of it falls out of this one idea. This chapter builds the mental model carefully, because everything after it assumes you have it.

## Why ownership exists

Think about what a garbage-collected runtime actually does. It lets you create references freely, share them freely, and stop thinking about them. The price is a runtime component that periodically walks your memory, figures out what is still reachable, and reclaims the rest. That bookkeeping is invisible in a small service and very visible in a latency-sensitive one: GC pauses, cache pressure from extra metadata, and a fleet of servers sized for the collector's headroom rather than your workload.

Manual memory management is the opposite trade. You get deterministic cleanup and full control, but the compiler trusts you completely. Off-by-one free, double free, returning a pointer to a stack frame that no longer exists — all of these compile in C and explode in production, sometimes months later, in a code path nobody has touched.

Rust refuses both compromises. The rule it enforces is small enough to write on an index card:

> Each value in Rust has a single **owner**. When the owner goes out of scope, the value is **dropped**. Moving or borrowing is the only way to access a value otherwise.

The compiler enforces that card statically. There is no garbage collector, and there is no manual `free`. Cleanup is deterministic — it happens at a precise, predictable moment, the instant a binding goes out of scope — and it happens even if that scope is exited early by a `return`, a `?`, or a panic unwinding.

## The stack and the heap

To understand moves, you need to be precise about where data lives. The **stack** is a LIFO region of memory tied to the call structure of your program. Pushing a stack frame is a pointer bump; popping one is a pointer bump back. Values with a known, fixed size — integers, booleans, floats, characters, fixed-size arrays, pointers themselves — live there. Access is nearly free because the address is computable from the frame pointer.

The **heap** is for everything whose size is not known at compile time, or that must outlive the current call. Allocation is a real operation: the allocator finds a free region, records it, and hands you an address. In Rust you rarely touch the allocator directly; instead, smart types like `String`, `Vec<T>`, and `Box<T>` own a heap buffer on your behalf.

Consider the difference between the two string types, because the distinction will follow you for the rest of your Rust life:

```rust
let n: i32 = 42;              // known size: lives on the stack
let s = String::from("book"); // heap-backed: lives on the heap
```

A `String` is a small struct of three machine words — a pointer to a heap buffer, a length, and a capacity. That triple lives on the stack; the characters `"book"` live on the heap. So when people say "a `String` is on the heap," the honest version is: *the buffer is on the heap, the handle to it is on the stack.* This picture — a small handle on the stack pointing at a buffer on the heap — is exactly what a *move* manipulates.

## Move semantics

Here is the sentence that surprises everyone coming from other languages: **assignment moves ownership in Rust; it does not copy.**

```rust
let s1 = String::from("book");
let s2 = s1; // ownership of the heap buffer moves to s2

// println!("{s1}");        // compile error: s1 no longer owns anything
println!("{s2}");
```

Under the hood, nothing was duplicated. The stack triple (pointer, length, capacity) was bitwise-copied from `s1`'s slot into `s2`'s slot, and then `s1` was marked invalid. Why invalidate it? Because when `s1` and `s2` go out of scope, Rust would otherwise insert two heap deallocations of the same buffer — a classic double free. Instead of tracking that with a runtime counter or collector, the compiler simply refuses to let two owners exist.

Types that are cheap to bitwise-copy — all the integers, floats, booleans, characters, and tuples or arrays made only of those — are marked `Copy`. They never move; assignment duplicates them, and the original stays valid:

```rust
let x: i32 = 42;
let y = x;      // i32 is Copy: a plain bitwise copy
println!("{x} {y}"); // both fine
```

When you *do* want a deep copy of a heap-backed value, you ask for it explicitly, so the cost is visible in the code:

```rust
let s1 = String::from("book");
let s2 = s1.clone(); // explicit deep copy of the heap buffer
println!("{s1} {s2}"); // both valid
```

That dot is one of the most important characters in the language. Wherever you see `.clone()`, you know a real allocation is happening — Rust makes expensive operations syntactically loud so they can't hide in a plain `=`.

## Ownership and functions

Passing a value to a function follows the same rule as assignment: by default, the value **moves** into the parameter. The caller loses access; the callee is now the owner and is responsible for dropping it — unless it hands ownership back.

```rust
fn consume(s: String) {
    println!("got {s}");
} // s dropped here

fn main() {
    let s = String::from("payload");
    consume(s);
    // println!("{s}"); // error: s was moved into consume
}
```

If a function needs to use a value and give it back, that's awkward but honest — and it is exactly the friction that motivates the next chapter. Returning values *out* of a function transfers ownership to the caller, which is why constructors like `String::from` work: the returned `String` is owned by whoever receives it.

```rust
fn make_greeting(name: &str) -> String {
    format!("hello, {name}") // ownership moves to the caller
}
```

A useful habit when reading Rust: track the *owner* of every heap value in a function. If a value flows into a call and you still need it afterward, you either need a borrow (next chapter) or a `.clone()`.

## Drop, RAII, and deterministic cleanup

When the owner of a value goes out of scope, Rust calls `drop` on it. For `String` that means freeing the buffer; for a `Vec` it means freeing its elements. You can observe the order with your own type:

```rust
struct Ticket(u32);

impl Drop for Ticket {
    fn drop(&mut self) {
        println!("releasing ticket {}", self.0);
    }
}

fn main() {
    let _a = Ticket(1);
    let _b = Ticket(2);
    println!("scope ending");
} // prints: scope ending, releasing ticket 2, releasing ticket 1
```

This pattern has a name older than Rust: **RAII** — resource acquisition is initialization, and cleanup is destruction. The power of it goes far beyond memory. A `File` closes its descriptor on drop. A `MutexGuard` releases the lock on drop. A socket, a thread handle's join state, a database connection wrapped in a pool guard — all of them release their resources in exactly one place: when their owner leaves scope. You cannot forget to call `close()` in Rust, because there is no `close()` to forget; there is only the end of the scope.

Contrast this with `try`/`finally` or `defer` discipline in other languages: in Rust the cleanup is attached to the *type*, not to each call site. Write the type once, and every future use of it is automatically exception-safe and early-return-safe.

One more nuance: `drop(value)` as a function is not callable directly — if it were, the value would be dropped twice. The standard library provides `std::mem::drop(value)` instead, which consumes the value immediately and ends its life right there. It is the idiomatic way to say "release this now, not at the end of the block."

## Box and putting values on the heap

The simplest heap-owning type is `Box<T>` — a single value on the heap with its handle on the stack. It has no refcounting, no locking, no runtime: it is a pointer with exactly one owner, and the compiler enforces that.

```rust
let b = Box::new(42);
println!("b = {b}"); // dereferences automatically when printed
```

Boxes show up in three everyday situations. First, **recursive types**, where a value can contain itself indirectly and therefore must live behind a pointer so its size stays finite:

```rust
enum List {
    Cons(i32, Box<List>),
    Nil,
}
```

Second, **trait objects** like `Box<dyn Error>` or `Box<dyn Draw>` — a pointer to "some type that implements this trait," with the concrete type erased; chapter 3 covers the mechanics. Third, **moving big values around cheaply**: moving a `Box` copies one machine word, not the payload.

The rest of the heap ecosystem builds on the same ownership idea: `Rc<T>` adds a *runtime* reference count for shared read-only access (with the compiler refusing to let you mutate through it), and `Arc<T>` is the thread-safe version you'll meet in chapter 5. Rust never made sharing illegal — it made the cost of sharing explicit and the rules of sharing checkable.

## Reading code with ownership in mind

Ownership changes how you *design*, not just how you compile. A few habits that pay off immediately:

- **Return owned values from constructors and builders.** The caller gets a self-contained value with no strings attached to your internals.
- **Take borrows as parameters whenever you don't need to keep the value** (`&str` instead of `String`); that keeps the caller's options open and avoids surprise moves.
- **Clone deliberately, never accidentally.** A `.clone()` at a hot path is a performance review comment; a `.clone()` at a cold path is a perfectly reasonable readability purchase.
- **Model resources as types with `Drop`.** If something must be released — a lock, a file, a transaction — wrap it so the release is structural.

The compile errors you will hit this week are the borrow checker teaching you this model. "Value moved here" is not the compiler being difficult; it is the compiler telling you that your mental sketch had two owners for one buffer, and that one of them was about to be wrong.

## Key takeaways

- Every value has exactly one owner; when the owner leaves scope, the value is dropped — deterministically, with no garbage collector.
- Assignment and by-value parameters *move* heap-owning values; `Copy` types duplicate instead, and `.clone()` is the explicit, visible deep copy.
- `Drop` and RAII attach cleanup to types, so locks, files, and sockets release correctly on every path, including early returns and panics.
- `Box<T>` puts one value on the heap; recursive types and trait objects are its everyday uses.
